definition: A lake's cheap object storage plus a warehouse's ACID transactions, schema, and performance — in one.
explanation: Open table formats layer a transaction log and metadata over Parquet files in object storage, so one store gives reliable tables, BI-grade queries, and direct ML access without copying data into a separate warehouse.
interviewLine: A lakehouse puts ACID tables, schema, and warehouse performance directly on lake storage via open table formats — one store for BI and ML.
whyItMatters: It removes the copy-to-warehouse step and the two-system split between BI and ML.
interviewQuestion: What problem with the lake-plus-warehouse setup does a lakehouse solve?

definition: File formats (Parquet) store data; table formats (Iceberg, Delta) add a metadata layer for tables.
explanation: Parquet/ORC define how bytes sit in one file. A table format (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi) tracks which files make up a table plus a transaction log — enabling ACID, schema evolution, time travel, and safe concurrent writes over those files.
interviewLine: Parquet is a file format (bytes in a file); Iceberg/Delta are table formats adding a metadata log over many files for ACID, evolution, and time travel.
whyItMatters: Confusing the two layers is common; the table format is what makes a lake behave like a warehouse.
commonMistake: Calling Iceberg a file format — it sits above Parquet, managing which files form the table.

definition: Bringing atomic, consistent transactions to append-only object stores that lack them natively.
explanation: S3/GCS have no multi-file transactions. Table formats add a transaction log: writers create new files and atomically commit a new metadata version pointing to them. Readers see a consistent snapshot; failed writes leave the table untouched.
interviewLine: Table formats bring ACID to object storage via a transaction log: writes stage files and atomically commit a new snapshot, so readers never see partial writes.
whyItMatters: ACID over cheap object storage is the core breakthrough that made lakehouses possible.
interviewQuestion: How does a transaction log provide atomicity when S3 itself can't?

definition: Databricks' table format: a transaction log (_delta_log) of JSON commits over Parquet files.
explanation: Delta records every change as an ordered commit in _delta_log, giving ACID, time travel, schema enforcement, and MERGE. Readers reconstruct table state from the log; it's tightly integrated with Spark/Databricks.
interviewLine: Delta Lake adds ACID and time travel via an ordered JSON transaction log (_delta_log) over Parquet, with schema enforcement and MERGE.
whyItMatters: Delta is one of the big three table formats and the default on Databricks.

definition: An open table format with hidden partitioning and engine-neutral metadata, backed by many vendors.
explanation: Iceberg tracks table state through metadata/manifest files and offers hidden partitioning — queries don't need to know the partition scheme, and you can evolve partitioning without rewriting data. It's engine-agnostic (Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake).
interviewLine: Iceberg is an open, engine-neutral table format with hidden partitioning and partition evolution, so queries and layout change without rewrites.
whyItMatters: Iceberg is winning as the open, vendor-neutral standard — the hot table-format topic.
interviewQuestion: What does Iceberg's 'hidden partitioning' free the query writer from?

definition: An upsert-first table format built for incremental writes and CDC ingestion.
explanation: Hudi optimizes for mutable data: fast upserts/deletes and incremental pulls of only changed records. It offers Copy-on-Write (read-optimized) and Merge-on-Read (write-optimized) table types, popular for streaming/CDC into a lake.
interviewLine: Hudi is upsert-first, tuned for CDC and incremental writes, offering Copy-on-Write and Merge-on-Read table types for read vs write optimization.
whyItMatters: Hudi is the third major format, chosen when upsert and CDC throughput dominate.

definition: Querying a table as it existed at a past snapshot or version, thanks to the transaction log.
explanation: Because every commit is versioned and old files are retained, you can read 'AS OF' a timestamp or version — for audits, reproducing an ML training set, or rolling back a bad write instantly.
interviewLine: Time travel queries a prior table version via the transaction log, enabling audits, reproducible datasets, and instant rollback of a bad write.
whyItMatters: Time travel is the lakehouse's standout feature — audit, reproducibility, and one-command rollback.
interviewQuestion: How would you use time travel to recover from a bad batch load?

definition: Enforcement rejects writes that violate the schema; evolution lets the schema change safely over time.
explanation: Enforcement blocks a write with wrong types/extra columns, preventing corruption (schema-on-write on the lake). Evolution allows controlled additions/renames tracked in metadata, so the table changes without rewriting history.
interviewLine: Enforcement rejects nonconforming writes; evolution permits controlled schema changes in metadata — safety plus adaptability on lake tables.
whyItMatters: Together they give a lake warehouse-grade safety while still adapting to change.

definition: A single statement that inserts new rows and updates matching ones — the workhorse of lake table writes.
explanation: MERGE INTO matches target rows on a key and updates them, inserts unmatched rows, and can delete — enabling CDC application, SCD Type 2, and idempotent loads on lakehouse tables that plain append can't do.
interviewLine: MERGE upserts in one statement — update matches, insert new, optionally delete — powering CDC, SCD2, and idempotent loads on lake tables.
whyItMatters: MERGE is how CDC and dedup land in a lakehouse; it's the reason table formats added upsert support.

example.content:
MERGE INTO customers t
USING updates s ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

definition: Merging many small files into fewer large ones (OPTIMIZE) to restore read performance.
explanation: Streaming and frequent writes create tiny files; opening thousands of them wrecks scan speed (the 'small files problem'). Compaction rewrites them into right-sized files, and old files are cleaned up (VACUUM) after retention.
interviewLine: Compaction (OPTIMIZE) merges many small files into large ones to fix the small-files problem that cripples scan performance.
whyItMatters: Small-file buildup is the top lakehouse performance killer; compaction is the standard remedy.
commonMistake: Never compacting a streaming-fed table — read latency degrades as file count explodes.

definition: Co-locating related data in the same files by sorting on high-cardinality columns to skip more data.
explanation: Z-ordering multi-dimensionally sorts data so rows filtered together sit in the same files. With per-file min/max stats, queries skip files that can't match — big gains when you filter on the clustered columns.
interviewLine: Z-ordering clusters related rows into shared files so, via file min/max stats, queries skip non-matching files — data skipping on the columns you filter.
whyItMatters: Z-ordering plus file stats is the lakehouse equivalent of a warehouse's clustering/sort keys.

definition: The metadata service that tracks tables, schemas, and permissions across engines — Unity, Glue, Nessie.
explanation: A catalog maps table names to their current metadata/location and governs access. Unity Catalog (Databricks), AWS Glue, and Nessie (git-like, versioned) let multiple engines share one governed view of lakehouse tables.
interviewLine: A catalog (Unity, Glue, Nessie) tracks table metadata, location, and permissions so many engines share one governed, discoverable view of the lakehouse.
whyItMatters: The catalog is what makes lakehouse tables discoverable, governed, and shareable across tools.
